These credits are strictly non-refundable, with no expenditure limit, and unused amounts may be carried back three years or forward 20 years.
1. Executive Summary and the 2024 to 2026 Legislative Transformation

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program constitutes the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and technological innovation in Canada. Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada—which formulates statutory tax policy—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—which oversees technical eligibility and financial compliance—the program delivers billions of dollars annually to businesses conducting systematic investigations in fields of science and technology within Canada. During the 2024–2025 fiscal year, the CRA delivered $4.5 billion in SR&ED investment tax credits (ITCs) across more than 19,000 corporate and individual claimants, encompassing over 22,000 processed claims. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, program utilization expanded further, with the CRA reporting $4.9 billion in ITCs claimed and $4.6 billion formally allowed, representing an expansion of approximately 50% in annual credit value since the 2022 fiscal year. Contrary to persistent industry perceptions that SR&ED claims face prohibitive rejection rates, empirical CRA administrative data from the most recent reporting cycle confirm that approximately 96% of processed SR&ED claims result in allowed tax credits: 90% of claims are accepted strictly as filed, 6% are accepted following financial or technical modifications, and only 4% are denied in their entirety.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most consequential statutory overhaul in more than a decade. Following nationwide stakeholder consultations initiated in Federal Budget 2024 to modernize Canada's innovation incentives, the Department of Finance released initial reform proposals on December 13, 2024, which were subsequently detailed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and translated into draft legislative amendments on August 15, 2025, with public comments invited through September 12, 2025. Those interim proposals initially contemplated raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10 million–$50 million corridor to $15 million–$75 million, extending the enhanced refundable credit to eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs), and reinstating the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs that had been repealed effective January 1, 2014.

On November 4, 2025, Canada's Minister of Finance and National Revenue, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, tabled Federal Budget 2025, titled Canada Strong, in the House of Commons. Budget 2025 superseded the interim $4.5 million proposal by fulfilling the federal commitment to increase the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC to $6.0 million, alongside major administrative reforms aimed at accelerating CRA review timelines and deploying artificial intelligence to streamline risk assessment. These legislative measures were codified in Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Consequently, the expanded SR&ED parameters are no longer mere policy proposals; they are binding statutory law applicable retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), while the capital property restoration applies to depreciable property acquired and available for use—and equipment lease costs first becoming payable—after December 15, 2024.

body.text: The structural implications of the Bill C-15 reforms fundamentally alter the financial calculus for mid-market technology firms, capital-intensive manufacturers, and publicly traded Canadian innovators. By doubling the enhanced expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $6.0 million and shifting the upper boundary of the phase-out window from $50 million to $75 million, Parliament eliminated the steep marginal tax penalty that previously deterred scaling Canadian companies from raising institutional growth equity, venture debt, or public market capital inside Canada. Simultaneously, the restoration of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs reverses a twelve-year policy exclusion that had disadvantaged hardware engineering, clean technology, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing enterprises relative to pure-play software developers.
2. Statutory Architecture of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The Canadian SR&ED regime is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Rather than operating as a discretionary ministerial grant program, the SR&ED framework functions as an entitlement-based statutory tax mechanism. Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada whose technical activities and related expenditures satisfy the statutory tests and strict filing deadlines is legally entitled to two distinct, interlocking fiscal incentives: the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 / Section 127.1 investment tax credit.

Under the first incentive mechanism, subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures—in computing income from the business for the taxation year in which the expenditures are incurred. Unlike ordinary business operating expenses deducted annually under section 9 and section 18, eligible SR&ED expenditures are accumulated in a dedicated statutory pool under subsection 37(1). Any portion of the Section 37 pool not deducted in the current taxation year may be carried forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in any subsequent taxation year. This indefinite carryforward grants corporate tax planners substantial flexibility to defer claiming Section 37 deductions in a given year in order to create sufficient Part I taxable income to absorb expiring foreign tax credits, charitable donations, or non-refundable investment tax credits. Conversely, subsection 37(2) of the Income Tax Act governs the current-year deduction of SR&ED expenditures carried on outside Canada, but it excludes salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for work outside Canada that is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer: under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), those amounts, capped at 10% of the taxpayer's salaries and wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada, are deemed to be for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Outlays governed by subsection 37(2) do not enter the indefinite subsection 37(1) carryforward pool and do not earn SR&ED investment tax credits.

Under the second incentive mechanism, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act entitle a taxpayer to earn an SR&ED investment tax credit calculated as a statutory percentage—either the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) or the 35% enhanced rate when combined with the 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1)—of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditures" incurred in the taxation year. Earned ITCs are first applied under subsection 127(5) to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Where unused ITCs remain after eliminating current-year Part I tax payable, eligible claimants may receive a direct cash refund under section 127.1—amounting to 100% of the unused enhanced 35% ITC earned on current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount, and 40% of the unused ITC earned on capital expenditures or qualifying 15% credits—or may carry the unused non-refundable ITC back 3 taxation years or forward up to 20 taxation years to offset Part I tax in those periods.

To prevent double taxation relief on the same dollar of expenditure, the Income Tax Act enforces a mandatory statutory synchronization mechanism between the deduction pool and the tax credit. Any SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in a taxation year—whether deducted against Part I tax payable under subsection 127(5) or refunded in cash under section 127.1—reduces the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e). If that subsequent-year pool reduction causes the Section 37 pool balance to become negative at the end of that following taxation year, the negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's business income for that following year pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(v).
The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal gateway to both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 investment tax credit is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" housed in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which consolidated the definition formerly located in Regulation 2900(1). In Canadian tax audit practice, a pervasive analytical error involves conflating section 127—which governs what constitutes a "qualified expenditure" once technical eligibility is already settled, or subsection 127(11.1), which reduces the claim for assistance—with subsection 248(1), which strictly defines what technical activities constitute SR&ED.

Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined in its preamble as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and is structured around four positive inclusion limbs—paragraphs 248(1)(a) through (d)—constrained by seven absolute statutory exclusions in paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k). Under the first two inclusion limbs, paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, while paragraph 248(1)(b) encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under the third inclusion limb, paragraph 248(1)(c) covers experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Over 90% of commercial SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under the experimental development limb. Crucially, the statutory text explicitly validates incremental improvements to existing products or processes, provided that the underlying work is undertaken to achieve a genuine technological advancement by resolving an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty, rather than merely achieving a commercial product enhancement through standard engineering.

Under the fourth positive limb, paragraph 248(1)(d) includes work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Consequently, activities such as computer programming, CAD drafting, data collection, and testing are never standalone SR&ED under Canadian law; they qualify solely under paragraph 248(1)(d) when they are commensurate with the needs of, and directly support, core basic research, applied research, or experimental development carried out in Canada.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) stipulate that SR&ED does not include work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection. Because these seven exclusions are written directly into the statutory text of subsection 248(1), they are non-arguable before the CRA or the Tax Court of Canada. Where an activity otherwise described in paragraphs (a) to (c) falls within paragraphs (e) to (k), it is statutorily excluded from SR&ED. For example, a data analytics or software development enterprise that applies established statistical models, known machine-learning libraries, or standard data-cleaning pipelines to new client datasets is performing excluded "routine data collection" under paragraph 248(1)(k) or routine engineering, regardless of the commercial complexity or labour hours expended on the engagement.

body.text: 3. Investment Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Phase-Out Mechanics

The quantum and cash refundability of a claimant's federal SR&ED investment tax credit are governed by four primary statutory variables: the legal classification of the taxpayer throughout the taxation year; the nature of the qualified expenditure (current expenditure and Prescribed Proxy Amount versus capital expenditure); whether the expenditure falls within or exceeds the corporation's annual expenditure limit; and the taxpayer's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average annual gross revenue.
Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations and the Six Million Dollar Expenditure Limit

A corporation that qualifies throughout the taxation year as a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) as defined in subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act—broadly, a private corporation resident in Canada that is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, one or more public corporations, or any combination thereof—is entitled to earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate (15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) plus the 20% additional rate under subsection 127(10.1)) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Consequently, an eligible CCPC incurring $6,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures (including the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount) earns $2,100,000 in enhanced ITCs, which is 100% refundable in cash under subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01) to the extent that the credit exceeds the corporation's Part I federal income tax payable. Where the CCPC incurs qualified capital SR&ED expenditures within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, those capital expenditures likewise earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate, but any unused portion of the credit is 40% refundable in cash—yielding an immediate 14% cash refund on the capital cost, while the remaining 21% non-refundable ITC is available to be carried back 3 years or forward 20 years against Part I tax.
The Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula under Subsection 127(10.2)

Under the default statutory rule in subsection 127(10.2), a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the combined "taxable capital employed in Canada" (within the meaning assigned by Part I.3 of the Income Tax Act, section 181.2) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (widened from the pre-reform $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 corridor).

Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC with a full 365-day taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024 that does not file the gross revenue election, the annual Expenditure Limit (EL) under subsection 127(10.2) is determined by the formula:

EL = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is the amount, if any, by which prior-year associated-group taxable capital employed in Canada (TC) exceeds $15,000,000 (EL is nil where TC is $75,000,000 or more)

Equivalently, for prior-year associated-group taxable capital (TC) falling within the phase-out corridor of $15,000,000 < TC < $75,000,000, every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1:

By contrast, for taxation years that began before December 16, 2024, the legacy formula under subsection 127(10.2) applied a $3,000,000 base limit phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada:
EL = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is the amount, if any, by which TC exceeds $10,000,000
Audit Fact-Check on the 2019 Repeal of the Taxable Income Phase-Out Factor

A recurring technical error in secondary commentary is the assertion that a CCPC's annual expenditure limit for the 35% SR&ED ITC is reduced when its prior-year taxable income exceeds $500,000 (historically phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year taxable income). In reality, Federal Budget 2019 permanently repealed the use of prior-year taxable income as a factor in determining a CCPC's annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2)—together with the consequential repeal of the amalgamation and wind-up continuity rules in paragraph 87(2)(oo) (replaced by paragraph 87(2)(j.6)) and paragraph 88(1)(e.8)—effective for all taxation years ending after March 18, 2019. Consequently, a highly profitable CCPC generating $25 million in prior-year taxable income—while maintaining less than $15 million in prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada—retains its full $6,000,000 expenditure limit and earns the full 35% ITC, with 100% refundability on current expenditures under subsection 127.1(2.01).

Prior-year taxable income does, however, retain a narrower statutory function under subsection 127.1(2) of the Income Tax Act: it determines whether a CCPC satisfies the definition of a "qualifying corporation", defined as a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) does not exceed its "qualifying income limit" of $500,000, which itself phases out as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada rises from $15 million to $75 million. If a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2), any basic 15% ITC it earns on qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of its $6,000,000 expenditure limit is 40% refundable in cash. Conversely, if a CCPC's prior-year taxable income exceeds the $500,000 qualifying income limit (rendering it a non-qualifying CCPC governed by subsection 127.1(2.01)), the corporation still receives 100% cash refundability on its 35% ITC for current expenditures up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (and 40% refundability on capital expenditures within the limit), but its 15% ITC earned on expenditures above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is entirely non-refundable.
Extension to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations under Subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127(10.6)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC to "eligible Canadian public corporations" (ECPCs) as defined in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must be resident in Canada, must be a public corporation (or would be one if a listing on any designated stock exchange, including one outside Canada, were taken into account), must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, and must not be controlled by any particular person if the shares held by non-residents were owned by that person.

Under new subsection 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act, an ECPC is entitled to an annual expenditure limit of up to $6,000,000. Unlike the default CCPC rule—which measures balance-sheet taxable capital—an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years ending before the current taxation year (determined using GAAP consolidated financial statements if the ECPC is a member of a consolidated group under subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.63) and subsection 233.8(1)) falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000:
EL = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − B) ÷ $60,000,000, where B is the amount, if any, by which three-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,000

Within its annual expenditure limit, an ECPC earns a 35% ITC that is 100% refundable on qualified current expenditures (and the Prescribed Proxy Amount) and 40% refundable on qualified capital expenditures. Any qualified expenditures incurred by an ECPC in excess of its expenditure limit earn the basic 15% ITC, which is strictly non-refundable.
The CCPC Average Gross Revenue Election under Subsection 127(10.31)

Recognizing that pre-revenue or early-commercialization deep-technology, biotechnology, clean-energy, and hardware CCPCs frequently raise substantial institutional share capital or venture debt—driving their Part I.3 "taxable capital employed in Canada" well above $15,000,000 while their actual operating revenues remain modest—Parliament enacted subsection 127(10.31) of the Income Tax Act. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a standalone CCPC (or an entire group of associated CCPCs filing jointly) may elect in prescribed form to have its annual expenditure limit determined using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue formula ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000) instead of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. Where a valid election is made under subsection 127(10.31) for a taxation year, the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) does not apply to the corporation or associated group for that taxation year. For a venture-backed CCPC that has raised $60 million in preferred equity (which would otherwise grind a taxable-capital-based expenditure limit down to $1.5 million) but has only $8 million in three-year average annual gross revenue, electing under subsection 127(10.31) restores the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit, preserving an additional $900,000 in annual cash refunds ($4.5 million × 20% rate differential).
Associated Corporations, Consolidated Groups, and Short Taxation Years

To prevent the artificial multiplication of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit through corporate fracturing, the Income Tax Act enforces strict aggregation and proration rules across corporate groups. Under subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.4), all CCPCs that are "associated" with one another in a taxation year under section 256 must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit, reduced by the combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (or combined three-year average gross revenue if an election is filed) of the entire associated group. The associated corporations must file an allocation agreement in prescribed form (Schedule 49, Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3). If any member of the associated group fails to file the agreement within 30 days after notice in writing by the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister allocates the expenditure limit among the group under subsection 127(10.4). Deeming rules under subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23) also empower the Minister to deem corporations to be associated where transactions are undertaken to avoid association status.

Parallel aggregation rules in subsections 127(10.61) through 127(10.63) require ECPCs that are members of the same consolidated group (as defined via subsection 233.8(1)) to share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit phased out using the consolidated group's three-year average annual revenue. Furthermore, where a CCPC or ECPC has a short taxation year of fewer than 51 weeks, its expenditure limit otherwise determined is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 under subsection 127(10.5) (which renumbered former subsection 127(10.6) effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024), while subsection 127(10.64) sets the parallel application rules for ECPCs, including short-year proration, the gross-up of revenue for short fiscal periods, and averaging over fewer than three fiscal years.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Methodologies, and Assistance Reductions

Once a project satisfies the technical eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable SR&ED expenditures under section 37 and its "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9). Under Canadian tax law, only five core categories of outlays qualify: salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED; overhead and other expenditures calculated via either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method; materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED; eligible SR&ED contract and third-party payments subject to the 80% ITC inclusion rule; and reinstated capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.
Salaries and Wages and the 2026 Specified Employee Caps

Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and Regulation 2900, a claimant may include the portion of salaries and wages paid to employees working in Canada (plus up to 10% of domestic SR&ED salaries for permissible foreign support work performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)) that is directly attributable to the time those employees spent directly engaged in SR&ED. Pursuant to subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any accrued salary, wages, or other remuneration that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year and is strictly disallowed until the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid.

The Income Tax Act draws a fundamental statutory distinction between regular arm's-length employees and "specified employees". Under subsection 248(1), a "specified employee" of a person is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—defined as a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any other corporation that is related to the corporation (counting shares owned by persons with whom the taxpayer does not deal at arm's length)—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, or sibling of a controlling shareholder).

For specified employees, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations enforce four stringent anti-avoidance restrictions tied to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), which for the 2026 calendar year is $74,600.00, alongside a Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) of $3,500.00, an employee and employer first-band CPP contribution rate of 5.95% outside Quebec, and a maximum first-band CPP contribution of $4,230.45 per employee and employer. First, under subsection 37(9), whereas regular arm's-length employees may have performance bonuses and taxable benefits included in their direct SR&ED wage claim in Part 3 of Form T661 (though excluded from the Part 5 proxy salary base), a specified employee is completely barred from claiming any bonus, remuneration based on profits, or taxable benefits as an SR&ED expenditure; similarly, dividends paid to shareholder-founders are never eligible SR&ED expenditures because dividends are distributions of after-tax corporate surplus rather than T4 employment income. Second, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee that can enter Part 3 of Form T661 for a taxation year cannot exceed 5 times the YMPE, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee divided by 365; for a taxation year ending in 2026, this direct salary ceiling is $373,000 (5 × $74,600). Third, under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations, when computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661, the amount includable for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of actual SR&ED salary claimed, 75% of the specified employee's total salary and wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) for the taxation year, and 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the year. For a full 365-day taxation year ending in 2026, the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling is $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600). Thus, if a founder-CTO spends 100% of their working time on eligible SR&ED and earns a regular T4 base salary of $260,000 in 2026, the corporation may claim $260,000 as a direct SR&ED wage in Part 3 (as it is below the $373,000 cap), but only $186,500 (the lesser of 75% × $260,000 = $195,000 and $186,500) enters the Part 5 proxy salary base to generate a 55% PPA of $102,575. Fourth, if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in the same year, the 5 × YMPE cap and 2.5 × YMPE proxy cap must be allocated across the associated group by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development) under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.5).
Overhead and Other Expenditures Under the Proxy Method and Traditional Method

In Section A of Part 3 of Form T661, a claimant must make an annual, irrevocable election for the taxation year between two mutually exclusive methodologies for claiming SR&ED overhead: the Proxy Method (selected on Line 160) or the Traditional Method (selected on Line 162). If a taxpayer fails to specify a calculation method on Form T661, the CRA defaults to processing the SR&ED claim under the Traditional Method.

Under the Proxy Method, the taxpayer does not specifically track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the taxpayer computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations. From an audit verification standpoint, any circulating guidance asserting that the federal proxy overhead rate is 65% or 60% is factually erroneous and reflects repealed law: under Regulation 2900(4), the PPA rate was 65% for years up to 2012, transitioned to 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014. Claiming a 65% proxy rate overstates the notional overhead by ten percentage points and triggers an automatic assessment adjustment. Furthermore, under Regulations 2900(5) through 2900(9), the Part 5 proxy salary base is narrower than gross payroll: it includes only basic T4 salaries and wages for time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, excluding taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the Income Tax Act, bonuses, profit-based remuneration, the employer's share of payroll taxes (CPP, QPP, EI, EHT, WCB), and specified employee salaries exceeding the 75% / $186,500 limits (even though the employer's share of payroll taxes and regular bonuses for non-specified employees remain claimable as direct SR&ED wages in Part 3). Because actual overhead expenses are already deducted as ordinary business operating expenses under section 9, the notional PPA does not enter the subsection 37(1) deduction pool; instead, it is added solely to the Part 4 qualified expenditure pool to earn the 15% or 35% ITC, subject to the Regulation 2900(6) overall cap.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method (paragraph 37(1)(a) and Regulations 2900(2)–(3)), no notional PPA is calculated. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, and substantiate every actual overhead and other expenditure that is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred but for the performance of the SR&ED—along with the portion of clerical and administrative support salaries directly attributable to SR&ED. This distinction governs the eligibility of cloud computing clusters, AI training infrastructure, and software or CAD subscriptions. Under the Proxy Method, cloud computing expenses and software subscriptions are never separately claimable because all overhead and computing infrastructure are conclusively represented by the 55% PPA; claiming them separately constitutes double counting. Under the Traditional Method, however, incremental cloud computing resources provisioned specifically to execute experimental development—such as dedicated GPU compute instances spun up solely to train and test experimental deep-learning models—qualify as directly related and incremental overhead, entering both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC base. Consequently, while salary-heavy engineering teams with modest infrastructure costs benefit from the low administrative burden of the 55% Proxy Method (for instance, five engineers with $600,000 in eligible salary generate $330,000 in notional PPA without tracking a single utility or server invoice), compute-intensive AI or data analytics firms whose dedicated cloud spend exceeds 55% of their SR&ED salary base should deliberately elect the Traditional Method on Line 162, supported by granular cloud billing telemetry. General-purpose SaaS tools and standard commercial CAD seats remain excluded under both methods.

body.text: Materials Consumed and Materials Transformed

Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and Regulation 2900(2)(a), a claimant may include 100% of the laid-down cost—comprising invoice cost, customs and excise duties, freight, and non-recoverable taxes—of materials that are either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass items destroyed, exhausted, or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials, such as chemical reagents, destructive metallurgical test coupons, and laboratory consumables. Materials transformed encompass raw materials or sub-components integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom testing apparatus constructed specifically to resolve technological uncertainties. Materials incorporated directly into commercial inventory sold in the ordinary course of business do not qualify unless they first constituted a genuine experimental prototype or pilot plant whose primary objective was resolving technological uncertainty. Furthermore, if property whose cost (or transformed materials) previously generated an SR&ED ITC is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the SR&ED recapture rules in subsections 127(27) through 127(35) claw back the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the statutory ITC percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion to commercial use), adding the recaptured credit directly to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable in the year of disposition or conversion.
Subcontractors, Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

Payments made for SR&ED performed on the claimant's behalf are governed by distinct statutory rules depending on the arm's-length relationship and geographic location of the performer. Where a claimant contracts with an arm's-length person or partnership to perform SR&ED on the claimant's behalf in Canada (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9)), 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in the Section 37 pool, but only 80% of the contract expenditure is included in "qualified expenditures" for calculating the 15% or 35% ITC—a statutory restriction enacted effective January 1, 2013 to exclude the contractor's presumed 20% taxable profit margin. Crucially, the subcontractor must perform the SR&ED work physically inside Canada; payments to foreign subcontractors or offshore development teams are completely ineligible for SR&ED ITCs. To withstand CRA audit scrutiny, the underlying contract statement of work and invoices must identify the specific eligible SR&ED (or paragraph 248(1)(d) support work) performed on the claimant's behalf in Canada and confirm that the claimant retained ownership of the resulting intellectual property or the right to exploit the results.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length (NAL) party (subsections 127(11.6)–(11.8) and 127(13)), payments made by the payer to the NAL performer do not qualify for ITCs in the hands of the payer unless the NAL performer and the payer jointly execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), which transfers the underlying actual qualified expenditures incurred by the NAL performer to the payer up to the contract price. Separately, third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii)–(iii)) made to an approved association, university, college, research institute, or non-profit SR&ED corporation in Canada to be used for SR&ED related to a class of business of the taxpayer (where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results) are 100% deductible under Section 37 and 80% eligible for federal ITCs.
Reinstated Capital Expenditures and Equipment Lease Costs After December 15, 2024

One of the most consequential pillars of Bill C-15 is the full reinstatement of pre-2014 eligibility for SR&ED capital expenditures and capital lease costs, applicable to depreciable property acquired (and becoming available for use) after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024. Under reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b) and amended subsection 127(9), a taxpayer may claim on Line 390 of Form T661 (Version 26) 100% of the capital cost of new or used depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024—such as laboratory instrumentation, testing rigs, experimental moulds and tooling, specialized servers, and pilot machinery—provided the property is intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada. When a depreciable asset is claimed as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390, 100% of its cost enters the Section 37 deduction pool (providing immediate 100% write-off) and therefore must be kept off Schedule 8 (Capital Cost Allowance) to prevent duplicate depreciation claims. Land remains excluded and, under paragraph 37(8)(e), buildings and leasehold interests in buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings) remain strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, although Federal Budget 2025 separately introduced temporary 100% immediate expensing under the CCA regime for newly acquired manufacturing and processing buildings where at least 90% of the building's floor space is dedicated to manufacturing or processing in Canada before 2030 (phasing down to 75% in 2030–2031 and 55% in 2032–2033). While qualified SR&ED capital expenditures earn the same headline ITC rates as current expenditures (35% within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit for CCPCs and ECPCs; 15% above the limit or for other corporations), the unused 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures is 40% refundable in cash under section 127.1 (rather than 100% refundable), with the remaining 60% of the credit carried back 3 years or forward 20 years against Part I tax.

In tandem with purchased capital equipment, Bill C-15 and Form T661 Version 26 restored the eligibility of equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024. On Line 350 of Form T661, under both the Proxy Method and Traditional Method, a claimant may claim 100% of lease costs for equipment used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture under the Proxy Method). Furthermore, on Line 355 of Form T661 (applicable under the Proxy Method only), if leased equipment (other than general office equipment or furniture) is used primarily (50% to under 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease costs is eligible to be claimed. Audit verification confirms that occasional secondary blog commentary claiming equipment lease payments were not restored is factually incorrect; both the Department of Finance legislative explanatory notes and Lines 350 and 355 of Form T661 Version 26 explicitly reinstate post-December 15, 2024 lease costs.
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(11.1), 127(18), and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act (and not subsection 37(2), which deals with SR&ED carried on outside Canada), both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool must be reduced dollar-for-dollar by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the time of filing in respect of the SR&ED. Government and non-government assistance defined in subsection 127(9) encompasses federal, provincial, or municipal grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, super-deductions, and provincial or territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Quebec CRIC, BC SR&ED credit, and Alberta IEG). If a claimant formally renounces a provincial R&D tax credit on or before the income tax return filing-due date, that renounced credit does not reduce the federal SR&ED pool. Conditional repayable government contributions—where periodic repayments depend on future product revenues, are subject to a ceiling, and terminate on a set date whether or not the full advance has been repaid—are likewise classified as government assistance upon receipt, with subsequent repayments becoming eligible SR&ED outlays only in the taxation year actually repaid. Similarly, when a Canadian business receives a "contract payment" from another taxable Canadian entity to perform SR&ED on that client's behalf, subsections 127(18) and 127(19) reduce the performer's qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar (down to nil for that project) so that only the paying Canadian client claims the ITC.
5. Judicial Precedents, Case Law Evolution, and Audit Substantiation Standards

While subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes the statutory text of SR&ED, Canadian federal courts have developed a binding body of common-law jurisprudence to adjudicate technical eligibility and evidentiary disputes between taxpayers and the Minister of National Revenue.
The Foundational Five-Question Test in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen

The foundational precedent of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is the decision of Judge Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC). Evaluating five hydraulic engineering physical modelling projects, Justice Bowman distilled the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) (and Information Circular IC 86-4R3) into a five-question judicial test that every claimant must satisfy on a balance of probabilities.

Under the First Question, the court asks: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman defined "routine engineering" as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field". If the resolution of a technical challenge is reasonably predictable using established engineering methodologies—even where the work is difficult, complex, or expensive—no technological uncertainty exists. Under the Second Question, the court asks: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Justice Bowman specified (at para. 16) that this requires a five-stage methodology comprising: (i) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (ii) the formulation of a clear objective; (iii) the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (iv) the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (v) the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Under the Third Question, the court asks: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses? Work conducted through haphazard trial-and-error or intuitive tinkering fails this requirement because it cannot isolate causal relationships. Under the Fourth Question, the court asks: Did the process result in a technological advancement (or was the overall approach adopted aimed at achieving a scientific or technological advancement)? Justice Bowman clarified that a technological advancement represents an advancement in general scientific or technological understanding to competent professionals in the field, and that proving systematically why a plausible hypothesis will not work advances technological knowledge just as validly as a successful build. Finally, under the Fifth Question, the court asks: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?
Appellate Entrenchment and the Evidentiary Burden in RIS-Christie Ltd. and C.W. Agencies Inc.

Shortly after Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) cemented Justice Bowman's analytical framework as binding national law. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890, 1998 CanLII 8876 (FCA), Justice Robertson analyzed the fifth criterion concerning contemporaneous documentation. The Federal Court of Appeal held that because repeatable testing and verification are intrinsic to scientific research, "evidence of scientific research must be adduced by the taxpayer in order to demonstrate that such research (including testing) was undertaken and that it is repeatable". While the absence of formal written records does not create a standalone statutory bar outside subsection 248(1), a claimant lacking objective records generated as the work progressed will almost invariably fail to discharge the evidentiary burden of proving systematic investigation and repeatability.

Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212 (at paragraph 17), the Federal Court of Appeal formally adopted and restated the five Northwest Hydraulic questions verbatim, confirming that all lower courts and CRA reviewers must apply this five-part test. Later Tax Court of Canada decisions, including Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 (at para. 37) and Clevor Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (at para. 11), explicitly reaffirmed that the five criteria are cumulative: "To be eligible for SR&ED, each of the questions in the five-factor test must be answered in the affirmative". Even after the CRA reorganized its administrative Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives in 2021–2022 around a two-requirement ("Why" and "How") structure, the Federal Court of Appeal and Tax Court of Canada confirmed that the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) remains the five-question framework established in Northwest Hydraulic.
Routine Engineering Versus Experimental Development in Zeuter Development, Jentel Manufacturing, Hypercube, and Joel Theatrical Rigging

Across multiple industries, the Tax Court of Canada has applied the Northwest Hydraulic criteria to police the boundary between routine commercial engineering and genuine experimental development. In Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, 2007 DTC 41 (at para. 20), Justice Little dismissed the taxpayer's appeal, holding that when technical uncertainties can be resolved by applying standard engineering practices, consulting equipment vendors, or following published technical specifications, the work does not constitute SR&ED. Similarly, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (Docket 2008-3875(IT)G, aff'd 2011 FCA 355), a plastic sheet thermoformer claimed SR&ED for developing a lighter, smaller storage system ("Multi-Bins") by testing aluminum components, three different mould casting materials, multiple groove iterations, and a heat sink. Justice D'Arcy dismissed the appeal with costs, ruling that thermoforming and injection moulding were well-known manufacturing processes and that iterating mould geometries or adding a heat sink without formulating and systematically testing scientific hypotheses to overcome a non-routine technological barrier constituted routine engineering that failed to demolish the Minister's assumptions.

In the software sector, the Tax Court in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, 2015 DTC 1089 (at para. 48) dismissed a claim involving the development of a web "crawler" program designed to read and analyze websites, holding that the claimant failed to distinguish between complex software coding using existing frameworks and overcoming genuine computer science uncertainties, and failed to link generalized employee task descriptions to documented hypothesis-testing cycles. Subsequently, in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed the appeal of a theatrical rigging contractor while delivering an authoritative doctrinal synthesis of SR&ED jurisprudence: acknowledging the scope of "routine engineering" (para. 17), defining a "hypothesis" under Question 2 as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" (para. 26), cataloguing the objective characteristics required to demonstrate the scientific method under Question 3 (para. 33), and synthesizing the case law on contemporaneous records under Question 5 (para. 46).
Recent Taxpayer Victory and Evidentiary Blueprint in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (Informal Procedure; judgment of Justice Bodie signed December 13, 2024, with amended reasons dated January 17, 2025, regarding the 2020 taxation year), the Tax Court of Canada provided a clear evidentiary blueprint for how small and medium-sized enterprises can defeat a CRA disallowance. The appellant undertook food-science experimentation to control microbial growth and prevent exploding cans in order to produce a vinegar-based beverage that remained shelf-stable at room temperature without pasteurization or refrigeration. The Minister of National Revenue disallowed the claim in full, alleging that the taxpayer merely utilized preservatives already known to competent professionals in the field, failed to conduct a systematic investigation, and lacked sufficient contemporaneous documentation.

Applying Northwest Hydraulic, C.W. Agencies, and Joel Theatrical Rigging, Justice Bodie allowed the taxpayer's appeal in full. On Question 1 (Technological Uncertainty), the Court held that even when individual ingredients or preservatives are known in the industry, their complex chemical and biological interactions within a specific unpasteurized beverage matrix created a genuine technological uncertainty—manifested by recurring microbial fermentation and exploding cans—that could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard food-science procedures. On Questions 2 and 3 (Hypotheses and Scientific Method), the Court found that the taxpayer formulated specific testable statements regarding preservative concentrations, pH levels, and microbial inhibition, and systematically tested and modified those hypotheses across sequential experimental trials. On Questions 4 and 5 (Technological Advancement and Records), the Court ruled that discovering the multi-variable formulation parameters that prevented microbial gas generation advanced general technological understanding, and that the appellant's progressive test logs discharged the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

body.text: 6. CRA Governance, Form T661 Version 26 Filing Architecture, and Audit Defence
Governing Bodies and Review Personnel

Unlike jurisdictions that divide R&D certification between a science ministry and a revenue authority, Canada vests both technical eligibility determination and financial expenditure verification within the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Within the CRA's SR&ED Directorate, claims selected for review are evaluated by two specialized cadres operating under published internal manuals, namely the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and the Financial Claim Review Manual. Technical eligibility is assessed by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—specialists holding degrees and industry experience in fields such as software engineering, chemical processes, biotechnology, or mechanical manufacturing—who review Part 2 of Form T661, conduct technical interviews or site visits, and determine whether the claimed work satisfies subsection 248(1) and whether claimed labour and materials are commensurate with the needs of the SR&ED. RTAs report to Research and Technology Managers (RTMs), who oversee the review process and must sign off on any report proposing claim adjustments. Concurrently, Financial Reviewers (FRs) audit Parts 3 through 6 of Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 against general ledgers, T4 payroll summaries, specified employee ownership registers, subcontractor contracts, capital asset invoices, and government assistance schedules to verify compliance with sections 37, 127, and 127.1.
Structural Anatomy of Form T661 Version 26 and Schedule T2SCH31

To access either the Section 37 deduction or the Section 127 ITC, a claimant must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporate claimants, or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA released Version 26 of Form T661 on May 15, 2026, which comprises 10 mandatory parts and integrates dedicated lines for reinstated capital expenditures and equipment lease costs. While claimants must complete Part 2 for each claimed project, a taxpayer claiming more than 20 projects in a taxation year may choose to submit Part 2 for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value at the time of filing, retaining Part 2 descriptions for the remaining projects to be provided upon CRA request (with failure to provide them resulting in automatic disallowance). Similarly, for classified government projects, claimants omit Section B of Part 2 from the filed return and retain the classified narrative alongside the authorization letter on file.

body.text: Mastering Technical Narratives on Lines 242, 244, and 246

An SR&ED claim succeeds or fails in Section B of Part 2 of Form T661. Because the CRA enforces strict word limits—350 words for Line 242, 700 words for Line 244, and 350 words for Line 246—narratives must concentrate on technical facts written in the precise engineering or scientific vocabulary of the qualified personnel who performed the work. On Line 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties – Maximum 350 Words), the claimant must articulate the specific technological barrier, system constraint, or knowledge gap that existed at the start of the project (or arose during execution) and explain why competent professionals in the field could not resolve that barrier using publicly available knowledge, standard design patterns, or routine engineering. Claimants must avoid business or commercial language and instead define the quantitative gap between existing technological capabilities and the required system state. On Line 244 (Work Performed in the Tax Year – Maximum 700 Words), the claimant must describe in chronological order the systematic investigation executed strictly within the taxation year being claimed, following a rigorous Hypothesis → Experiment/Analysis → Quantitative Results → Logical Conclusion/Modification structure that demonstrates how variables were isolated, tested, and analyzed. On Line 246 (Technological Advancements – Maximum 350 Words), the claimant must state the new technical knowledge, boundary conditions, or underlying scientific principles discovered through the investigation in Line 244, directly linked back to the uncertainty in Line 242—recognizing that proving why a tested hypothesis cannot succeed under specific physical or computational constraints constitutes a valid advancement in technological knowledge.
The Absolute Eighteen-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) (for the Section 37 deduction pool) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for the Section 127 ITC), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a), the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For individuals operating sole proprietorships whose T1 return is due June 15, the SR&ED deadline is 17.5 months after the December 31 year-end, while partnerships filing a T5013 Partnership Information Return must file Form T661 no later than 12 months after the earliest filing due date of any partner for the tax year in which the partnership's fiscal period ended.

Crucially, subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act prohibits the Minister of National Revenue from extending the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline. If a corporation files Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31 even one day after the 18-month deadline (unless the deadline falls on a weekend or CRA-recognized public holiday, in which case it moves to the next business day), the expenditures are deemed not to be SR&ED expenditures and no ITC is earned. Moreover, once the 18-month deadline has passed, no additional projects or expenditures may be added, and a claimant is strictly barred from substituting alternative expenditures to make up for amounts disallowed during a CRA audit. Consequently, filing the SR&ED claim alongside the original T2 return at the 6-month mark accelerates cash refunds while preserving a 12-month window prior to the 18-month bar to file amended forms if additional eligible projects or costs are uncovered.
The April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process and CRA Service Standards

Historically, the CRA maintained processing service standards of 60 calendar days for refundable claims accepted as filed, 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for technical or financial review, and 365 calendar days for non-refundable claims selected for review, supplemented by non-binding educational tools such as the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), Pre-Claim Consultations (PCC), Pre-Claim Project Reviews (PCPR), the Account Executive (AE) service, and the post-filing First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS). Effective April 1, 2026, pursuant to Federal Budget 2025, the CRA launched a formal Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process alongside expanded artificial intelligence risk-triage algorithms. Under this new process, businesses may obtain up-front technical approval of their eligible SR&ED projects prior to filing their tax return, and for claims passing through this elective stream that subsequently require a financial expenditure review, the CRA's processing standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. Simultaneously, increased AI risk modelling in CRA administration shields low-risk claims from unnecessary audit interventions while the CRA conducts targeted consultations to modernize Form T661.
Claim Preparer Penalties and the Four-Tier Dispute Resolution Protocol

To police compliance among external SR&ED consultants, Part 9 of Form T661 requires mandatory disclosure of every claim preparer who accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim, including their Business Number, billing arrangement (such as contingency fee percentage, flat fee, or hourly rate), and total fee charged. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if complete and accurate prescribed information is omitted from Part 9, a mandatory $1,000 penalty applies, for which the corporate claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable. In cases involving false statements or gross negligence, subsection 163(2) imposes taxpayer gross-negligence penalties of 50% of the overstated credit, while section 163.2 imposes third-party civil penalties directly against culpable tax preparers.

Where a disagreement arises during a CRA review, claimants should navigate a four-tier escalation protocol: first, submitting a targeted technical and documentary rebuttal to the RTA's draft SR&ED Review Report or Financial Reviewer's Proposal Letter; second, escalating unresolved disputes to the overseeing Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and Financial Review Manager (or requesting an Administrative Second Review); third, filing a formal Notice of Objection (Form T400A) with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 calendar days of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment under section 165 to trigger an independent review by an Appeals Officer and independent Appeals Science Advisor; and fourth, appealing an adverse Appeals decision (or after 90 days of inaction) to the Tax Court of Canada under section 169 via either the Informal Procedure or General Procedure.
7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Multi-Jurisdictional Stacking
Statutory Interaction of Provincial Credits and Federal Assistance Grinding

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, eight Canadian provinces and one territory provide dedicated corporate R&D tax credits for qualifying expenditures incurred at a permanent establishment within their borders. With the sole exceptions of Quebec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA]), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA and claimed via provincial schedules filed with the federal T2 return. Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(11.1) of the federal Income Tax Act, every provincial and territorial R&D tax credit constitutes "government assistance" that reduces both the federal Section 37 deduction pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar (unless formally renounced by the T2 filing-due date) before the federal 35% or 15% ITC is computed.
Ontario R&D Tax Incentives: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario operates three complementary corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566), provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to CCPCs on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), yielding up to $240,000 in cash refunds. The OITC rate was reduced from 10% to 8% effective June 1, 2016, and its $3,000,000 expenditure limit phases out when prior-year associated-group taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508), provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% effective June 1, 2016) available to all corporations with no expenditure limit and a 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward period. While the OITC, ORDTC, and federal SR&ED ITC do not reduce the expenditure base for the OITC, any OITC and OBRITC claimed in the year do reduce the qualified expenditure base used to compute the 3.5% ORDTC. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedules 568 and 569 (T2SCH568 & T2SCH569), provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified payments made under an eligible R&D contract with an approved Ontario university, college, hospital research institute, or prescribed research centre, capped at $20,000,000 in annual contract expenditures ($4,000,000 maximum credit).
Quebec Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)

Quebec administers its corporate R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec (CO-17 corporate return). For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec replaced its legacy R&D credit framework with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC). The CRIC is 100% refundable for all corporations (having repealed the legacy $50M–$75M total asset phase-out) and provides an enhanced 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible Quebec R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above the statutory employee exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable rate on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier. In addition to core R&D salaries, subcontractors, and capital property, the CRIC extends eligibility to downstream pre-commercialization activities such as product certification testing and industrial design.
British Columbia and Alberta R&D Tax Regimes

In British Columbia, corporations with a BC permanent establishment claim the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit on Schedule 425 (T2SCH425), which provides a 10% fully refundable tax credit to CCPCs up to their $3,000,000 expenditure limit ($300,000 maximum refund) and a 10% non-refundable tax credit (3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward) for non-CCPCs and CCPC expenditures above the limit. In Alberta, corporations with an Alberta permanent establishment claim the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) independently on AT1 Schedule 29 filed with the Alberta AT1 return. The IEG provides a 100% refundable credit on up to $4,000,000 in annual eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (shared among associated corporations, yielding up to $800,000 per year), calculated as an 8% base rate on all eligible expenditures up to $4,000,000 plus an additional 12% incremental rate (for a 20% combined rate) on expenditures exceeding the corporation's baseline average Alberta SR&ED spending over the preceding two taxation years. The Alberta IEG phases out on a sliding scale for corporations with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 and is eliminated at $50,000,000.
Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial R&D Tax Credits

Among the remaining provinces and territories, Saskatchewan (Schedule 403) offers a 10% refundable credit for CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures and a 10% non-refundable credit above $1,000,000 or for non-CCPCs (up to a $10,000,000 total expenditure cap). Manitoba (Schedule 380) provides a 15% credit that is 7.5% refundable and 7.5% non-refundable for in-house SR&ED (and 15% fully refundable for contracts with eligible post-secondary institutions). In Atlantic Canada and the North, Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301—distinct from Schedule 305, which is the Newfoundland and Labrador Capital Tax on Financial Institutions reported on Line 518 of Schedule 5) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all corporations with no expenditure cap, while Yukon (Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable credit (increasing to 20% on payments to Yukon University). Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not levy a statutory T2 R&D tax credit.

8. Strategic Audit Conclusions and Compliance Recommendations

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 fundamentally reshaped the strategic and financial architecture of research and development tax incentives in Canada for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To capture the full fiscal value of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, public corporation refundability, and capital property restoration while insulating filings against CRA technical and financial adjustments, corporate taxpayers and R&D tax practitioners should institutionalize a comprehensive six-part governance framework.

First, scaling Canadian-controlled private corporations that have raised substantial institutional equity or venture debt—pushing their prior-year Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada above the $15,000,000 phase-out threshold—should systematically model their three-year average annual gross revenue prior to filing. Where three-year average gross revenue falls below the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out trajectory of taxable capital, executing the prescribed election under subsection 127(10.31) prevents erosion of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Second, hardware, clean technology, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing claimants should document the acquisition and available-for-use dates of SR&ED capital property and the dates on which equipment lease costs first become payable, claiming qualifying property acquired after December 15, 2024 on Line 390 (keeping it off Schedule 8) and equipment lease costs at 100% on Line 350 (≥ 90% SR&ED use) or 50% on Line 355 under the Proxy Method (50% to < 90% SR&ED use).

Third, with the Prescribed Proxy Amount fixed at 55% of the eligible salary base under Regulation 2900(4) (and capped for specified employees at $186,500 in 2026 under Regulation 2900(7)), artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-intensive enterprises whose dedicated cloud compute clusters exceed 55% of their direct SR&ED salary base should evaluate electing the Traditional Method on Line 162, backed by automated cloud resource tagging that isolates experimental training runs from commercial production workloads. Fourth, claimants relying on predictable cash flow—particularly newly eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs) and mid-market CCPCs claiming near the $6,000,000 ceiling—should leverage the CRA's April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process to secure up-front technical project validation and compress post-filing expenditure review timelines from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. Fifth, rather than reconstructing technical narratives retrospectively at year-end, engineering and scientific teams must embed the Northwest Hydraulic and Manning Canning evidentiary standards directly into their development workflows, documenting technological uncertainties (Line 242), testable hypotheses and controlled experimental iterations (Line 244), and quantified advancements in technical understanding (Line 246) contemporaneously within version-control commits, lab notebooks, and issue-tracking systems as the work progresses. Finally, because subsection 220(2.2) prohibits any administrative extension beyond the 18-month statutory reporting bar in subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m), corporations should file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 concurrently with their T2 return at the 6-month mark, verifying that Part 9 claim preparer disclosures are complete to eliminate exposure to the subsection 162(5.1) $1,000 penalty while preserving a full 12-month window for technical or financial amendments.
